content:
The image shows a corn stalk at close range, focused on the lower stalk/crown area. Key observations:

- **Affected part**: Lower stalk/node area near the soil line
- **Visual features**: Dark brown to black, wet/water-soaked rotted tissue at a node; the stalk appears soft and mushy at that point; there is visible dark discoloration and what appears to be oozing/slimy material
- **The outer rind of the stalk** is still green above the infected zone, but the node area shows dark, wet, collapsed tissue
- **No foul odor visible**, but the water-soaked, soft, dark brown/black node tissue is very prominent
- **Vascular strands** appear to still be somewhat intact within the rotted area

Comparing to candidates:
- **Bacterial_Stalk_Rot**: Water-soaked, tan to brown, soft and mushy lower internodes; dark, wet tissue; foul odor; vascular strands remain intact — matches well
- **Physoderma_Stalk_Rot**: Black nodes that snap easily — the blackening at the node here is consistent, but Physoderma typically shows clean black nodes without the wet/mushy appearance
- **Pythium_Stalk_Rot**: Soft, brown, water-soaked internode near soil line — also a close match, but typically a single internode collapses with plant remaining green/turgid

The prominent wet, dark, mushy rotting at the node with water-soaked tissue strongly points to **Bacterial_Stalk_Rot**. The tissue looks slimy and collapsed at the node, consistent with bacterial soft rot causing foul-smelling maceration of the pith with intact vascular strands.
